chapters.title: Gravity & Orbits
chapters.blurb: One inverse-square law, three laws of Kepler, and the handful of formulas every mission designer carries in their head: how fast, how long, how far, and how much velocity change (Δv) it costs to go somewhere else.

chapters.title: Rockets
chapters.blurb: A rocket is a machine for throwing mass backwards very fast. These equations say how much speed that buys, why we build rockets in stages, and what the atmosphere and gravity take back on the way up.

chapters.title: Atmosphere & Re-entry
chapters.blurb: Air thins exponentially with height, sound has a speed limit, and a capsule coming home at 11 km/s turns its kinetic energy into a shock layer hotter than the surface of the Sun.

chapters.title: Spacecraft Engineering
chapters.blurb: Once a spacecraft is flying, the problems change: talking across billions of kilometres, living off sunlight that fades with distance, staying neither too hot nor too cold, surviving radiation, and pointing and pushing with tiny forces for years.

chapters.title: Light & Stars
chapters.blurb: Almost everything we know about stars arrives as light. Temperature sets the colour, size and temperature set the power, distance dims it, and motion shifts it.

chapters.title: Telescopes & Optics
chapters.blurb: A telescope does two jobs: it collects light and it resolves detail. Aperture sets both, the atmosphere spoils the second, and cameras, adaptive optics and planet-wide arrays are how astronomers fight back.

chapters.title: The Sun & Space Weather
chapters.blurb: Our star is a variable magnetic furnace. Its light sets the solar constant; its differential rotation winds up magnetic fields; its wind, flares and coronal mass ejections buffet Earth's magnetosphere and the technology that depends on it.

chapters.title: Exoplanets
chapters.blurb: More than 5 000 planets are now known around other stars. A handful of equations turn a faint dip or a tiny wobble into a planet's size, mass, temperature and gravity — and frame the question of whether anyone lives there.

chapters.title: Relativity & Black Holes
chapters.blurb: Moving clocks run slow, clocks deep in gravity run slower, and enough mass in a small enough space closes off a region of spacetime entirely. Satellite navigation depends on all of it.

chapters.title: Cosmology
chapters.blurb: The Universe is expanding. A few equations connect the redshift of distant galaxies to the size, age, density and temperature of the whole cosmos.

legend.desc: Attractive force between the two bodies

equations.meaning: Every mass pulls on every other mass along the line joining them. Double either mass and the pull doubles; double the distance and it falls to a quarter. The same law drops an apple, holds the Moon in orbit and shapes galaxies. Isaac Newton published it in the Principia (1687).

equations.title: Kepler's first law — orbits are ellipses

legend.desc: Distance from the focus (the Sun) to the planet
Semi-major axis (half the long axis of the ellipse)
Eccentricity: 0 is a circle, close to 1 is a long thin ellipse

equations.meaning: Planets do not move in circles. Johannes Kepler found in 1609, from Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars, that each orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus — not at the centre. The closest point is $r_p = a(1-e)$ (perihelion) and the farthest is $r_a = a(1+e)$ (aphelion).

example.text: Mars: $a = 1.5237$ AU, $e = 0.0934$. Perihelion is at $\theta = 0$.

answer.text: about 206.7 million km; at aphelion Mars is 1.666 AU away — a 21 % swing.

equations.title: Kepler's second law — equal areas in equal times

legend.desc: Area swept per second by the Sun–planet line
Sun–planet distance
Angular speed around the Sun
Gravitational parameter of the central body

equations.meaning: A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Close to the Sun the line is short, so the planet must move fast; far away it crawls. Physically this is conservation of angular momentum, and it gives the speed ratio $v_p/v_a = (1+e)/(1-e)$ between perihelion and aphelion.

equations.title: Vis-viva equation

legend.desc: Orbital speed at distance $r$
Standard gravitational parameter of the central body
Current distance from the centre of the central body
Semi-major axis of the orbit

equations.meaning: The single most useful equation in orbital mechanics. It is conservation of energy for an orbit: kinetic plus potential energy per kilogram is fixed by the orbit's size, $-\mu/2a$. Know where you are ($r$) and which orbit you are on ($a$) and you know your speed. A circle ($r = a$) and an escape trajectory ($a \to \infty$) are special cases.

legend.desc: Speed at which kinetic energy equals the depth of the gravity well

equations.meaning: Throw something at this speed (ignoring air) and it coasts away forever, slowing down but never quite stopping. equations.title: Hohmann transfer Δv

legend.desc: Burn at departure (periapsis) and arrival (apoapsis)
Radii of the starting and target circular orbits
Gravitational parameter of the central body
Transfer time (half the transfer ellipse's period)

equations.meaning: Walter Hohmann showed in 1925 that the cheapest two-burn route between circular orbits is half an ellipse that just touches both. Burn prograde to stretch the orbit, coast half an orbit, burn again to circularise. It is slow but fuel-efficient, and it is how most satellites reach geostationary orbit and how Mars missions are timed.

equations.title: Roche limit

legend.desc: Closest distance (centre to centre) a moon can orbit without being torn apart
Radius of the primary (planet or star)
Mean densities of the primary and the satellite

equations.meaning: Closer than this, the difference in the planet's pull across a moon (the tide) beats the moon's own gravity, and a moon held together only by gravity comes apart. Édouard Roche computed it in 1848. A rigid body survives closer in; a fluid rubble pile breaks up farther out. Saturn's bright rings lie inside Saturn's Roche limit, and comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 was shredded passing inside Jupiter's in 1992.

legend.desc: Distance of L1 (or L2) from the smaller body

equations.meaning: L1 and L2 are the two points on the line through a star and planet where a spacecraft can orbit the star in lock-step with the planet: gravity and the rotating frame's centrifugal effect balance. For a small mass ratio both sit about one Hill radius from the planet. The Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) watches the Sun from Sun–Earth L1; the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) hides from it at L2.

equations.title: Synodic period
equations.aka: How often two orbiting bodies line up

legend.desc: Synodic period: time between successive identical alignments
Orbital periods of the two bodies around the same centre

equations.meaning: Two runners on a circular track: the faster one laps the slower one at a rate equal to the difference of their angular speeds. That is why Mars comes to opposition — and Earth–Mars launch windows open — only every 26 months, and why the lunar month (new Moon to new Moon) is two days longer than the Moon's true orbit. The closer the two periods, the longer the wait.

equations.aka: Why the Moon shows us one face (order of magnitude)

equations.meaning: The planet raises tidal bulges on the satellite; if the satellite spins, friction drags the bulges off the planet–satellite line and the planet's gravity pulls them back, slowing the spin until the same face always points inward. equations.title: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation

legend.desc: Change in velocity the rocket can achieve (no gravity or drag)
Specific impulse of the engine
Standard gravity, 9.806 65 m/s²
Effective exhaust velocity, $I_{sp}g_0$
Initial (fuelled) and final (empty) mass

equations.meaning: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published this in 1903 and it rules all of rocketry. Because each kilogram of propellant must also accelerate the propellant still on board, Δv grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio. Doubling Δv means squaring the mass ratio — the 'tyranny of the rocket equation'.

example.text: An RS-25-class engine in vacuum ($I_{sp} = 452$ s) on a stage that is 75 % propellant ($m_0/m_f = 4$).

equations.meaning: Thrust has two parts. The big one is momentum: mass thrown back each second times its speed. The second is a pressure imbalance across the nozzle exit. equations.meaning: Drag grows with the square of speed and in direct proportion to air density. legend.desc: Velocity lost to gravity during the burn

equations.meaning: Every second a rocket spends climbing, gravity steals $g\sin\gamma$ metres per second of the velocity its engines produce. Only tiny black holes would be hot enough to evaporate within the age of the Universe.

equations.meaning: Global Positioning System (GPS) clocks sit higher in Earth's gravity well, so general relativity makes them run fast by about 45.7 μs a day; their orbital speed makes them run slow by about 7.2 μs a day. The net is about +38 μs/day. Light travels 11 km in 38 μs, so without correction positions would drift by kilometres every day. The satellite clocks are deliberately tuned slightly slow before launch.

equations.meaning: Newton's gravity predicts closed ellipses; the tug of other planets makes Mercury's orbit turn slowly, 532″ per century. In 1859 Urbain Le Verrier found 43″ per century left unexplained, and astronomers even searched for a planet "Vulcan". In November 1915 Albert Einstein computed this formula from general relativity and got exactly the missing 43″ — he later said the result gave him heart palpitations. The same effect has since been measured for the star S2 orbiting the Milky Way's black hole.

equations.title: Friedmann equation
equations.latex: \begin{aligned} H^2 &= \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{k c^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\\ H(z) &= H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r(1+z)^4 + \Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_k(1+z)^2 + \Omega_\Lambda}\end{aligned}

equations.meaning: Alexander Friedmann derived this from general relativity in 1922. It is the energy budget of the expanding Universe: the expansion rate is set by what the Universe contains. Because radiation dilutes as $(1+z)^4$, matter as $(1+z)^3$ and dark energy not at all, each dominated in turn — radiation first, then matter, and now dark energy, which is making the expansion speed up.

equations.meaning: Set curvature and dark energy to zero in the Friedmann equation and solve for the density: that is the critical density, the dividing line between a Universe that would recollapse and one that expands forever. Cosmologists quote everything as a fraction of it ($\Omega = \rho/\rho_c$). Observations say the total is within a fraction of a per cent of 1: space is flat.

equations.meaning: Run the expansion backwards at a constant rate and everything meets after $1/H_0$ — the natural clock of cosmology. The real age differs because the expansion first slowed (matter) and then sped up (dark energy); by coincidence the two nearly cancel in our Universe (13.8 vs 14.5 Gyr). Measurements disagree: the cosmic microwave background (CMB) with ΛCDM gives 67.4, while the SH0ES distance ladder of Cepheids and supernovae gives 73.0 km/s/Mpc. This "Hubble tension" is one of the biggest open questions in cosmology.

equations.meaning: Light from a redshift-$z$ galaxy left when the Universe was $1/(1+z)$ of its present size. How long ago that was depends on the whole expansion history, so it is an integral over the Friedmann equation — computed here numerically (Simpson's rule, in the scale factor) each time you move a slider. Integrating all the way to $z \to \infty$ gives the age of the Universe: 13.79 billion years for the Planck 2018 parameters.

equations.title: Angular-diameter distance
equations.aka: Why the most distant galaxies look bigger

legend.desc: Line-of-sight comoving distance (distance today to where the light was emitted)

Physical size of an object and the angle it covers

equations.meaning: In an expanding universe "distance" has several meanings. The light we see from a distant galaxy left it when the galaxy was much closer to us, so its angular size corresponds to that smaller distance, $D_A$. Beyond $z \approx 1.6$, $D_A$ actually shrinks: more distant galaxies look larger again. The same integral fixes the angle of the sound-wave pattern in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), one of the most precise measurements in cosmology.

example.text: Planck 2018 parameters; a galaxy 10 kpc across.

answer.text: Mpc — so 1″ spans 8.2 kpc and a 10 kpc galaxy covers only 1.2″.
